summary: The 3GPP found cases where SIP private header fields (P-headers) from RFC 7315 need to appear in messages where RFC 7315 did not allow them. This informational document updates RFC 7315 to allow that, and it obsoletes RFC 7976.

plainLanguage.summary: Some special labels were only allowed on certain envelopes. Mobile phone standards needed them on more envelopes, so the rules were relaxed.

questions: what does rfc 9878 change in rfc 7315
subtitle: Loosens and corrects which SIP messages may carry the 3GPP private P-headers from RFC 7315.

tldr.problem: RFC 7315 contradicted itself about where SIP P-headers may appear, and the 3GPP found cases that need them in requests and responses where RFC 7315 did not allow them.
tldr.mechanism: This document replaces the usage statements in Section 5.7 of RFC 7315 with corrected text, for example allowing P-Access-Network-Info and P-Charging-Vector in ACK requests triggered by 2xx responses.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 7315 and obsoletes RFC 7976, whose change (P-Visited-Network-ID in responses) is carried forward.

today: RFC 9878 is an Informational document that updates RFC 7315 and obsoletes RFC 7976. The unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why RFC 7315 Needed Updating
sections.content:
The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) identified cases where SIP private header fields, the P-headers defined in RFC 7315, need to appear in SIP requests and responses where RFC 7315 did not allow them. This document updates RFC 7315 to allow that.

It also fixes misalignments. RFC 7315 contained contradictory statements: Section 5.7 did not match the definitions and usage in Section 4. The RFC says these misalignments arose when RFC 3455 was updated and then obsoleted by RFC 7315. Allowing P-Called-Party-ID in PUBLISH requests was deliberate in RFC 7315, so it is not counted as a misalignment.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook said two different things about where some labels could go. This update makes the rules agree and lets phone networks use the labels where they need them.

sections.title: Misalignments and 3GPP Use Cases
sections.content:
The fixes for misalignments are: remove REGISTER as a place for P-Associated-URI; delete responses as a place for P-Called-Party-ID and add the REFER method; allow P-Access-Network-Info, P-Charging-Vector and P-Charging-Function-Addresses in responses; and state that P-Charging-Vector cannot appear in ACK. For P-Visited-Network-ID, the clarification is that it cannot appear in NOTIFY, PRACK, INFO and UPDATE, and can appear in all non-100 (Trying) responses.

Two 3GPP use cases drive further changes. P-Access-Network-Info can carry Network Provided Location Information (NPLI), which the IP Multimedia Subsystem needs for correct billing. When a proxy triggers a bearer modification on seeing an SDP answer in a 2xx response to an INVITE, the NPLI must go in the ACK request, which RFC 7315 did not allow.

P-Charging-Vector carries the transit-ioi parameter that identifies transit operators. Each request may take a different transit path, so the header needs to be in every request and response, including ACK. In both cases the header MUST NOT be included in ACK requests triggered by non-2xx responses (the text says it shall not).
sections.plainLanguage: When a call changes, the phone company needs to know where you are and which carriers passed the call along, so it can bill correctly. The final "got it" message needed to carry that information too.

sections.title: The Replacement Text for RFC 7315
sections.content:
Section 3 replaces the usage statements in Section 5.7 of RFC 7315. In the new text:

  • P-Associated-URI appears in REGISTER 2xx responses.
  • P-Called-Party-ID appears in INVITE, OPTIONS, PUBLISH, REFER, SUBSCRIBE and MESSAGE requests.
  • P-Visited-Network-ID appears in all requests and associated non-100 responses, except in ACK, BYE, CANCEL, NOTIFY, PRACK, INFO and UPDATE.
  • P-Access-Network-Info and P-Charging-Vector appear in all requests and associated non-100 responses, except CANCEL requests, CANCEL responses, and ACK requests triggered by non-2xx responses.
  • P-Charging-Function-Addresses appears in all methods and associated non-100 responses, except CANCEL requests, CANCEL responses and ACK requests.

The change from RFC 7976 is that any response other than 100 (Trying) may include P-Visited-Network-ID, which is why this document obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rule list says, header by header, which kinds of messages may carry it and which may not.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
Security considerations remain those of RFC 7315, including sending information only to trusted entities, and they now also apply to the newly allowed messages. P-Access-Network-Info may carry privacy-sensitive information such as the user's location, so allowing it in ACK requests carries considerations similar to those for other requests in Section 6.4 of RFC 7315.

Disallowing a header where it was previously allowed causes no security issue, but implementers must be aware that other implementations may not have been updated, and must act sensibly if a header appears or is missing where it should not or should. There are no IANA actions. Because P-headers are mainly used in 3GPP networks where these updates are already defined in TS 24.229, the RFC sees no backward-compatibility concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Location details are private, so the same care applies now that they can ride on one more kind of message.
